To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
EBV infection of normal human B lymphocytes induces a DNA damage response that triggers OSR and cell senescence.

EBV uses the polycomb system to epigenetically repress the expression of key OSR genes and that the virus uses a unique mechanism for recruiting the polycomb system that involves the EBV nuclear antigen EBNA3A.

EBV infection of normal human B lymphocytes triggers OSR, and that EBV encodes two proteins that target the polycomb repressive system for the epigenetic repression, and hence the silencing, of the OSR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that allow EBV to establish a persistent infection in the human host and the consequences of these mechanisms for cellular physiology and pathobiology.
how EBV and other viruses that can trigger OSR have evolved mechanisms for counteracting these cell intrinsic defense mechanisms.
the molecular mechanisms by which EBV and other viruses manipulate cellular pathways and networks in order to establish a persistent infection and to promote cell proliferation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EBV has developed a highly sophisticated epigenetic solution for the OSR problem.
EBV has developed a highly sophisticated epigenetic solution for overcoming OSR.
EBV uses the host polycomb protein system to epigenetically repress OSR genes, thereby allowing infected B cells to survive, proliferate, and become transformed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EBV has evolved a polycomb-mediated epigenetic solution for the problem of OSR triggered by infection.
EBV uses a combination of epigenetic repression and viral protein-mediated degradation of key OSR components to establish latency in normal human B cells.
EBV has evolved to use the host polycomb system as a “molecular toolbox” to repress transcription of key genes in OSR and thereby to ensure the survival and proliferation of the infected cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EBV has evolved an elegant solution to the problem that OSR can be triggered by infection.
the virus uses a combination of epigenetic and genetic mechanisms to control the OSR, and that these mechanisms are likely to be relevant for understanding the biology of EBV and other viruses.
viruses have evolved a polycomb-mediated epigenetic solution for the problem of OSR.
